explanations.battle-of-abancay--battle-of-las-salinas: Abancay’s own article carries the link forward from its aftermath: Almagro released Hernando Pizarro on a promise, and “this proved to be a mistake as the Pizarro brothers and Alvarado raised another army and in less than a year faced Almagro yet again in a struggle for power at Las Salinas, in April 1538.” The prisoners Abancay put in Almagro’s hands, and the terms on which he gave them back, are what the article gives as the reason there was a second army in the field at all. `precondition-of` and not `caused`: the article makes the release a mistake, not Las Salinas its consequence. `probable`, because the only source the atlas can open here is the article (rule 22).
explanations.battle-of-acajutla--battle-of-tacuzcalco: Both articles make the second battle the sequel to the first's outcome rather than the next thing that happened. Acajutla: "Defeated, the Nahuat forces retreated to reassemble further along his route. In a second battle a few days later, the remaining formal Cuzcatlan army again assembled on the battlefield but was finally defeated." Tacuzcalco, from the other side: "On 8 June 1524, Alvarado fought and defeated Cuzcatlan fighters under Atlácatl at the Battle of Acajutla", and then "On 13 June 1524, Alvarado engaged Atlácatl in a second battle at Tacuzcalco. Atlácatl's army was larger than the army he commanded at Acajutla." Precondition of: the retreat and the reassembly are what put a larger Cuzcatlán army at Tacuzcalco five days later, and neither article says the first battle caused the second — it is the same army, regrouped.
explanations.battle-of-agnadello--battle-of-the-citad: The Vicenza article begins its account at Agnadello: "In May 1509, after the crushing defeat suffered in the Battle of Agnadello, the Venetian army seemed destined to fall with the Republic of Venice." The citadel of Vicenza was imperial in November because Agnadello had taken Veneto away from Venice in May. `precondition-of`: the article gives Agnadello as the condition the year was fought under, and Padua as the turn that opened Vicenza. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.battle-of-agnadello--siege-of-crema-1514: The Crema article says why the town was worth a siege: "Crema remained heavily militarized, serving as a Venetian bridgehead to reclaim territories lost after Agnadello", and again, of the Senate, "determined to recover all territories lost post-Agnadello". The loss at Agnadello is the condition that made Crema a Venetian bridgehead and therefore a target. `precondition-of` and not `caused`: the article makes Agnadello the state of affairs the siege happened inside, not its trigger. Probable: Wikipedia, with the work Wikipedia itself cites for the sentence beside it — which is a second author and not a second reading, so the confidence does not rise.
explanations.battle-of-agnadello--siege-of-padua--pre: The Siege of Padua article makes Agnadello the state Venice defended Padua from: Maximilian's army "did not reach Padua until mid-September, which allowed the Venetian commander Niccolò di Pitigliano to concentrate what remained of Venice's army after Agnadello, as well as several companies of volunteers from Venice, in the city." The Agnadello article says what that remnant was left by: "Faced with the continued advance of the French army, he hurriedly retreated towards Treviso and Venice. Louis then proceeded to occupy the remainder of Lombardy." `precondition-of` rather than `caused`: the defeat in May is the position the September defence begins from, and neither article says Agnadello brought the siege about — Maximilian raised his army in answer to Venice retaking Padua in July. Probable: Wikipedia alone, at two revisions.
explanations.battle-of-algiers-1541--italian-war-of-1: Francis I had promised not to declare war on Charles V for as long as the Emperor was campaigning against Algiers; the campaign collapsed in November 1541 and the declaration followed in July 1542. “Italian War of 1542–1546”, at revision 1370624570, § Prelude: “By the end of September, Charles was in Mallorca, preparing an attack on Algiers; Francis, considering it impolitic to attack a fellow Christian who was fighting the Muslims, promised not to declare war for as long as the Emperor was campaigning. The Imperial expedition, however, was entirely unsuccessful; storms scattered the invasion fleet soon after the initial landing, and Charles had returned to Spain with the remainder of his troops by November.” The second author, “Battle of Algiers (1541)” at revision 1375834500, § Expedition, is where the campaign ends: “Charles could not depart for the open sea until 23 November … He finally reached Cartagena, in southeast Spain, on 3 December.” The type is `enabled` because the article makes the forbearance conditional on the campaign rather than on its outcome: the condition lapsed and the war that the same paragraph then reports was free to begin. It is not read as `caused` — the Prelude gives Francis’s own reasons, Milan and Rincon’s murder, and Ottoman promises of aid, and the failure at Algiers is not among them. `probable`, on the articles alone (rule 22).
explanations.battle-of-andalien--battle-of-penco--rea: The Penco article opens its history on the defeat a month earlier: "After toqui Ainavillo's defeat in the Battle of Andalien, he gathered tens of thousands of warriors from the Arauco and Tucapel regions to reinforce his depleted 15,000 man army for an attack on de Valdivia's new settlement at Penco." The second attack is the same commander answering the first battle, on the article's own account. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.battle-of-cajamarca--battle-of-vilcacong: The Vilcaconga article opens its own account of the battle with Cajamarca and makes the connection in the same breath: “The Spanish emerged as victors in the Battle of Cajamarca in November 1532. Some 180 Spaniards under Francisco Pizarro were in control of major parts of the vast Inca Empire and held its emperor, Atahualpa, hostage.” What follows is the mechanism: “The Incas still controlled large territory including their capital Cuzco, and commanders who had been ordered to stand down by a captive Atahualpa now moved south toward the Spanish, able to rally tens of thousands of soldiers. The Spanish, for their part, sought to conquer Cuzco and add it to their territory.” So Cajamarca put the emperor in Spanish hands and set the Spanish on the road to Cuzco, and Quizquiz fortified the pass at Vilcaconga across that road. `precondition-of` and not `caused`: the article says Cajamarca gave the Spanish the hostage and the advance that brought them to the pass, not that it brought the battle at the pass about — the Inca decision to fight there is the article's, and the Incas' own. Probable: Wikipedia alone at one revision, and the only work the article cites for the section is a chapter by John F. Guilmartin with no page and no identifier, which rule 13 will not take as a source record. The two events are siblings under `spanish-conquest-of-the-inca-empire`, so A14's bar on an edge from a parent to its own child does not reach this one.
explanations.battle-of-cajamarca--conquest-of-tunis-1: The campaign against Tunis was paid for with Atahualpa’s ransom, and the Tunis article says so. “Conquest of Tunis (1535)”, at revision 1375228138, § Background: “The expense involved for Charles V was considerable, and at 1,000,000 ducats on par with the cost of Charles’ campaign against Suleiman on the Danube. Unexpectedly, the funding of the conquest of Tunis came from the galleons sailing in from the New World, in the form of two million gold ducats extracted by Francisco Pizarro for releasing the Inca king Atahualpa, whom he nevertheless executed on 29 August 1533.” That sentence names the ransom and the two men but not the event this atlas holds, so the second author is what joins them: “Battle of Cajamarca”, at revision 1370108415, opens “The Battle of Cajamarca … was the ambush and seizure of the Incan ruler Atahualpa by a small Spanish force led by Francisco Pizarro, on November 16, 1532” — the seizure for whose release the ducats were extracted. The type is `enabled`: the money is a condition the first article states plainly and is not offered as the reason Charles went to Tunis, which the same section gives as the Ottoman fleet at Tunis threatening Italy and Spain. `probable`, on the two articles alone (rule 22).
explanations.battle-of-cempoala--la-noche-triste--pre: Beating Narváez is what let Cortés go back to Tenochtitlan with an army large enough to hold it, and it is that return the night flight ends. The La Noche Triste article's § Cortés heads off Spanish punitive expedition: "Cortés marched to the coast, where he defeated the Cuban expedition led by Pánfilo de Narváez sent to capture him. When Cortés told the defeated soldiers about the riches of Tenochtitlan, they agreed to join him. Reinforced by Narvaez's men, Cortés headed back to Tenochtitlan." The Battle of Cempoala article's own § Aftermath reads the outcome the same way: "Velázquez, instead of eliminating Cortés as he had planned, essentially replenished and reinforced the army of his nemesis." `precondition-of`: the reinforced army is what was in the city to be driven out of it, and neither article makes the battle the cause of the flight. Probable: Wikipedia alone, at two revisions.
explanations.battle-of-cusco--battle-of-maraycalla--p: The Maraycalla article states the condition in its first sentence: the battle "was fought in 1534 between Spanish conquistadors and renegade forces of the Inca Empire ... whose capital Cuzco had been taken by the Spaniards in November 1533. The Inca army was commanded by famous general Quizquiz." Quizquiz is the commander who withdrew from Cusco in November 1533, and Maraycalla is the Spanish pursuit of him. `precondition-of`: the loss of the capital is the state of affairs the 1534 battle is fought from, and the article claims no more than that. Probable: Wikipedia alone, and the article carries a {{refimprove}} tag of its own.
explanations.battle-of-cusco--siege-of-cusco--precond: The siege article names this battle as the thing the siege was raised against: "A Spanish expedition led by Francisco Pizarro had captured the Inca capital of Cusco on November 15, 1533 after defeating an Inca army headed by general Quisquis", and from there its Background runs straight to Manco Inca's rebellion — the coronation the month after, Juan Pizarro's humiliations and imprisonment of Manco, and the flight of April 1536. The lead says what the siege was for: "The Incans hoped to restore their empire (1438-1533) with this action." precondition-of: Spanish possession of Cusco is the state of affairs the siege set out to undo, and the article argues the rebellion from how the Spaniards held the city rather than from the battle itself. Probable, and with a second author: the capture is cited there to Hemming, The Conquest of the Incas, p. 115, the Macmillan 1993 edition the article bibliography names.
explanations.battle-of-inaquito--battle-of-jaquijahua: Jaquijahuana’s article states what Iñaquito left behind it: Gonzalo Pizarro “crushed the army of Blasco Núñez Vela, who was decapitated on the field of battle. This, in its turn, ensured a struggle for the control of Peru between Gonzalo Pizarro and the royal forces.” Jaquijahuana is where that struggle was decided, by the same article’s account, and the viceroy’s death at Iñaquito is why the crown sent de la Gasca in his place. `precondition-of` and not `caused`: the article gives the defections at Jaquijahuana, not Iñaquito, as what settled it. `probable`, because the only source the atlas can open here is the article (rule 22).
explanations.battle-of-lagunillas--battle-of-millarap: The Millarapue article opens on the previous battle: "After the victory of the Spanish arms in the Battle of Lagunillas, Mendoza went into the hostile territory of Arauco looking for a decisive battle." The advance into Arauco that produced Millarapue three weeks later is, on the article's own account, what the victory at Lagunillas led to. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.battle-of-las-salinas--battle-of-chupas-: Chupas’s own article gives Las Salinas as the reason its loser raised an army: “Desperate not to face the same fate as his father after the battle of Las Salinas, Diego de Almagro II gathered an army of supporters.” Almagro the elder was captured at Las Salinas and executed in July 1538; the son’s fear of the same end is what the article says put the Almagrist force at Huamanga in 1542. `precondition-of` and not `caused`: four years and the assassination of Francisco Pizarro stand between them, and the article turns Chupas itself on Vaca de Castro’s governorship. `probable`, because the only source the atlas can open here is the article (rule 22).
explanations.battle-of-millarapue--battle-of-quiapo--: Millarapue is where Caupolicán's resistance to Mendoza failed, and Quiapo is where the toqui who replaced him made his stand. The article: "Caupolicán led the Mapuche unsuccessfully resisting the advance of Hurtado de Mendoza by attacking him from ambush in the Battle of Millarapue", after which Mendoza "built the fort and city of Cañete de la Frontera", Caupolicán attacked it, "was eventually betrayed and captured in the mountains" and executed. Then: "the manner of the death of Caupolicán inspired the Mapuches to continue the struggle with a guerrilla war", and "In Quiapo, the Mapuches under their new toqui, Caupolicán the younger, constructed a fort that was to stop the forces of Mendoza from marching into Arauco and rebuilding a fort there." Precondition-of: the article makes the execution, not the battle, what inspired the next round.
explanations.battle-of-novara-1513--battle-of-la-mott: The Novara article ends: "The French defeat forced Louis XII to withdraw from Milan and Italy." The La Motta article begins from what that withdrawal left Venice holding: "The Venetian commander, Bartolomeo d'Alviano, unexpectedly left without French support, retreated into the region of Veneto, pursued closely by the Spanish army under Ramón de Cardona." `precondition-of`: being without the French ally is the state the October battle begins from; neither article says Novara brought La Motta about. Probable: Wikipedia alone, at two revisions.
explanations.battle-of-novara-1513--battle-of-marigna: The Marignano article names Novara as what the 1515 campaign was fought to undo: "The campaign of Marignano followed years of Swiss successes, during which French fortunes in northern Italy had suffered greatly. The Swiss had taken control of Milan (for France the gateway to Italy) after their victory at the Battle of Novara (1513), and returned to its ducal throne Maximilian Sforza, son of Ludovico Sforza, to make Milan a protectorate of Switzerland." The Novara article says the same from its own end: "The French defeat forced Louis XII to withdraw from Milan and Italy." `precondition-of`: Swiss-held Milan is the position Francis I crossed the Alps against, which is the article's own account and stops short of saying the battle caused the campaign. Probable: Wikipedia alone, at two revisions.
explanations.battle-of-novara-1513--siege-of-dijon--e: The Dijon article opens its § Prelude with the claim: "After the French defeats at Novara (6 June) and Guinegatte (16 August), Louis XII anticipated a counter-attack by the Imperial armies on France’s own soil." Novara is the defeat that emptied Italy of the French army — la Trémoille was recalled from Italy to govern Dijon — and the invasion of Burgundy came three months later. `enabled` and not `caused`: the article says the defeat opened France to a counter-attack, not that it made this siege inevitable. Probable: Wikipedia alone, and the sentence carries no citation of its own.
explanations.battle-of-otumba--fall-of-tenochtitlan--: Surviving Otumba is what left Cortés an army to come back with. The Battle of Otumba article's lead: "The result of the battle was a successful defense for the Spanish, which allowed Cortés to reorganize his army, having suffered heavy casualties a few days before during his army's retreat from the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan, now known as La Noche Triste. A year later, by reinforcing his army with new men and supplies, and starting an alliance with the Tlaxcala Confederacy, Cortés found a way to reenter Tenochtitlan." The Fall of Tenochtitlan article credits the same thing: Cortés "knew how to use the military initiative that he gained after the battle of Otumba." `enabled` and not `caused`: the articles make the battle what made the siege possible, not what brought it about — the year between them was spent on men, supplies and the Tlaxcalan alliance. Probable: Wikipedia alone, at two revisions.
explanations.battle-of-pavia--war-of-the-league-of-co: The War of the League of Cognac article opens its background on this edge in so many words: "Shocked by the defeat of the Kingdom of France in the Italian War of 1521, Pope Clement VII, together with the Republic of Venice, began to organize an alliance to drive Charles V from the Italian Peninsula. Francis I, having signed the Treaty of Madrid, was released from his captivity in Madrid and returned to France, where he quickly announced his intention to assist Clement. Thus, on 22 May 1526, the League of Cognac was signed." The Battle of Pavia article says the same from its own end: Francis was taken to Spain, signed the Treaty of Madrid of 1526, and "denounced the treaty after his liberation and soon re-opened hostilities over Burgundy and Milan." An alliance organised because of a defeat, by a pope shocked by it and a king released from the captivity it caused, is a reaction to that defeat and not a consequence of it, so `reacted-to` and not `caused`. Probable, because both articles are read at one revision each and neither names a historian for the reading.
explanations.battle-of-penco--battle-of-tucapel--prec: Penco is where Concepción was founded and held, and Concepción is the base the southern forts were planted from — which is what the Mapuche council of 1553 resolved to make war over. The article: after Penco, "Despite the resulting submission of the local tribes, de Valdivia sent an emissary to the Viceroy of Peru, asking for additional forces", then Imperial, Villarrica and Valdivia are established and "de Valdivia returned to his base at Concepción in 1552". Then: "With the goal of securing the lines of communication with the southern forts, de Valdivia launched a third expedition which established forts at Tucapel, Purén, Confines, and Arauco... In 1553, the Mapuches held a council at which, because of the growth of Spanish forces in their territory, they resolved to make war" — and Lautaro opened it by attacking the fort at Tucapel. Precondition-of, over several steps the article names: the reason given for the war is the growth of Spanish forces, and Penco is where that growth was based.
explanations.battle-of-peteroa--battle-of-mataquito--: The Mataquito article makes Peteroa the reason the Spanish could take the field: "In early 1557, following the defeat and retreat of Lautaro after the Battle of Peteroa, Francisco de Villagra felt strong enough to gather a strong force of soldiers and march south to aid the remaining cities against the Mapuche besetting them." Enabled and not caused: the article gives Peteroa as what made the march possible, not as what the march answered. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.battle-of-polesella--battle-of-ravenna-1: The War of the League of Cambrai article takes the line from the one to the other in three stated steps. After Polesella: "Faced with a shortage of both funds and men, the Senate decided to send an embassy to Julius in order to negotiate a settlement", concluded on 15 February 1510. Then: "By concluding peace with the Venetians, the pope effectively left the League of Cambrai", and, "increasingly concerned by the growing French presence in Italy", "the Pope hired an army of Swiss mercenaries, ordering them to attack the French in Milan; he also invited Venice to ally with him against Louis." The Ravenna article is the French army fighting that alignment: Nemours "was determined to force the main army of the Holy League into battle". `enabled` and not `caused`: Polesella is what pushed Venice to the settlement that turned the Pope against France, and the article makes the reversal of alliances, not the river defeat, what put the two armies at Ravenna. Probable: Wikipedia alone, at two revisions.
explanations.battle-of-puna--spanish-conquest-of-the-: The Puná article opens by placing the battle where the conquest begins: it was "a peripheral engagement of Francisco Pizarro's conquest of Peru", and "The battle marked the beginning of Pizarro's third and final expedition prior to the fall of the Inca Empire." The article's last paragraph has the Spaniards sail from Puná "bound for more fruitful conquests on the Peruvian mainland". `precondition-of`: the expedition that became the conquest starts here, which is a condition of it and not its cause. Probable, and with a second author: Prescott, at pp. 142-143 in the edition the article cites.
explanations.battle-of-punta-quemada--spanish-conques: The Punta Quemada article claims the link in its lead: "Though it marked the end of Francisco Pizarro's first tentative expedition along the Pacific coast, the battle also represented a crucial step to Spain's discovery and conquest of the Peru." `precondition-of` and not `caused`: a crucial step towards a conquest begun seven years later is a condition of it, and the article argues nothing stronger. Probable, and with a second author: Prescott's History of the Conquest of Peru is the work the article rests on throughout, at pp. 96-102 for this battle.
explanations.battle-of-quiapo--battle-of-angol--preco: Quiapo is the defeat that produced the toqui who died at Angol, and the article says so at both ends. After Quiapo: "Soon after the defeat at Quiapo, the surviving leaders gathered and elected Illangulién as the new toqui. With most of the nations' warriors dead or wounded and the population decimated by the effects of war, starvation, and disease, he decided to retreat into the marshes of Lumaco and there gather their strength and train a new generation of warriors for a future revolt." At Angol: "Lorenzo Bernal drove the Mapuche army out of their pucara and pursued them down to the river and pushed them back into it, killing Illangulién and a thousand of his men." Precondition-of: Quiapo is what the army destroyed at Angol was raised in answer to.
explanations.battle-of-quilacura--battle-of-andalien-: Quilacura is what told Valdivia the force he had was not enough, and the expedition he came back with is the one that fought at Andalién. The article: "Pedro de Valdivia himself set out in 1546, with sixty horsemen plus guides and porters. Crossing the Itata River, he was attacked by Mapuche warriors in the Battle of Quilacura near the Bío-Bío River. Realizing that it would be impossible to proceed in such hostile territory with so limited a force, de Valdivia elected to return to Santiago after finding a site for a new city at what is now Penco." Then: "In 1550, a new expedition was launched, consisting of a naval force under Pastene, and a land force of two hundred Spaniards mounted and foot" — and it is that column which "camped for two days between the river and a lake, where they were attacked on the second night" at Andalién. Precondition-of: the defeat did not bring the second expedition about, it settled what size it had to be.
explanations.battle-of-ravenna-1512--battle-of-novara: The Novara article opens its § Prelude on Ravenna in so many words: "The French had been victorious at the Battle of Ravenna the previous year. Nevertheless, the French under King Louis XII were driven out of the city of Milan the following month by the Holy League. Following the French removal from Milan, Swiss mercenaries installed Maximilian Sforza as Duke of Milan on 29 December 1512." Novara was the French attempt to take Milan back: "In June 1513, the French army, consisting of more than 20,000 under Louis de la Trémoille, besieged the city of Novara, which was held by Swiss mercenaries." `precondition-of`: a victory that cost the French Milan a month later is the position the 1513 campaign begins from, which is what the article says and no more. Probable: Wikipedia alone, at two revisions.
explanations.battle-of-reynoguelen-1536--arauco-war--: The battle's own article places it before the war and inside its causation in one sentence: "This battle is an antecedent of the Arauco War." It is the first fighting between Spanish conquistadors and the Mapuche, ten years before the war this atlas dates from 1546 — which is why Wikidata's P361 filing under the war was refused here and this edge written instead. Precondition-of and not caused: an antecedent is what the article claims, and a battle at the confluence of the Ñuble and the Itata does not bring about a war that starts a decade later; it is what the war was already under way from.
explanations.battle-of-the-spurs--siege-of-dijon--ena: The same sentence of the Dijon article’s § Prelude names the second defeat: "After the French defeats at Novara (6 June) and Guinegatte (16 August), Louis XII anticipated a counter-attack by the Imperial armies on France’s own soil." Guinegatte of 16 August 1513 is the Battle of the Spurs, which the article links under that name. `enabled`, for the reason the Novara edge gives. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.battle-of-tucapel--battle-of-marihuenu--: The Marihueñu article makes the Spanish defeat at Tucapel the start of the sequence: "After the defeat at the Battle of Tucapel, the Spanish had hurriedly reorganized their forces, reinforcing fort La Imperial for its defense and abandoning Confines and Arauco in order to strengthen Concepción... It was only in February 1554 that he succeeded in putting together an army of 8,000 men, just in time to confront a punitive expedition under the command of Francisco de Villagra at the Battle of Marihueñu." The punitive expedition is the reorganisation Tucapel forced. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.battle-of-tucapel--battle-of-mataquito--: The Mataquito article states the motive in its lead: the battle "is notable for ending Mapuche designs on Santiago, while also avenging the death of former governor Pedro de Valdivia, who had been killed by Lautaro's warriors four years earlier." Valdivia's capture and death is what the Tucapel record is, on that article's own lead, so the avenging is a reaction to it. Probable: Wikipedia alone.
explanations.battle-of-ugentana--battle-of-ugentana-1: The second attack on Ugentana happened because the first one had not finished the job, and the article about the second says so in its own words. “Battle of Ugentana (1536)”, at revision 1373045056, § The Battle: “In 1535, the Portuguese captain of Malacca Dom Estevão da Gama attempted to defeat the Sultan of Johor by attacking his capital at Ugentana. Although he burned the city, the sultan avoided the total destruction of his forces by evacuating the city and retreating with his army into the jungle, while most of his fleet was out at sea at the time. Hence, he was able to rebuild his city and continue harassing the navigation of Malacca after the Portuguese had left, and for that reason Dom Estevão was compelled to try and attack Ugentana once more.” The same section carries the mechanism twice more, in the state the first attack left the ground in: the Portuguese found “a new stockade where a stone fort they destroyed the previous year had once stood”, and “the sultan’s forces were considerably weakened because the Portuguese had captured large amounts of artillery the previous year.” The second author is the record at the other end of this edge, “Battle of Ugentana” at revision 1373042668, which states the half the first article is reasoning from: “Unable to oppose the Portuguese, the sultan ordered the evacuation of the fort and also his capital under the cover of the night, and fled into the jungle”, and the city “was then burned”. `caused`, running forward from the incomplete victory to the campaign sent to complete it; `probable`, on the two articles alone, which rule 22 keeps below `consensus`.
explanations.battle-of-vilcaconga--battle-of-cusco--e: The Vilcaconga article makes the link itself and in one sentence: "Vilcaconga ensured that the Spanish would not be stopped on their way to the Incan capital, Cuzco. It was captured in the Battle of Cuzco and Pizarro entered the city in triumph on November 15, 1533." The same section says the combined force of de Soto and Almagro "managed to rout Quizquiz's forces and press further towards Cuzco". `enabled` and not `caused`: the article says the road to Cuzco was held open, not that Vilcaconga brought the capture about. Probable: Wikipedia alone at one revision — the only work the article cites, a chapter by John F. Guilmartin with no page and no identifier, cannot be written as a source record under rule 13.
explanations.capture-of-malacca-1511--attack-on-binta: There was nothing for the Portuguese to attack on Bintan until they had taken Malacca: the island was where the sultan they had driven out rebuilt, and the attack of 1521 was aimed at that. “Attack on Bintan (1521)”, at revision 1372970515, § Background: “In 1511, the governor of Portuguese India Afonso de Albuquerque captured the Malay city of Malacca. The Sultan of Malacca Mahmud Shah fled with his forces to Bintan Island and established his rule there. He built a new city and fleet there, and continuously harassed Portuguese Malacca and its shipping, Mahmud never gave up the idea of recapturing Malacca from the Portuguese and he constantly attacked Malacca with raids from 1517 to 1520”. The second author is the article the record at the other end already cites, “Capture of Malacca (1511)” at revision 1373484620, which states the same chain from the other end: “Afterwards, Mahmud moved to Bintan, an island kingdom south-east of Singapore that he usurped to wage war on the Portuguese in Malacca, harassing the city, its trade and sabotaging their diplomatic relations with China, until the Portuguese eventually devastated Bintan in 1526”. `precondition-of` and not `caused`: the capture of Malacca is what put a hostile court on Bintan and made it a target, while what the article gives as the immediate occasion is the raids of 1517 to 1520 and the destruction of Pago in 1520, neither of which this atlas holds. `probable`, on the articles alone, which rule 22 keeps below `consensus`.
explanations.capture-of-malacca-1511--siege-of-malacc: The 1551 siege was a siege of Portuguese Malacca, and Malacca was Portuguese because of 1511. “Siege of Malacca (1551)”, at revision 1375742313 — the revision this record cites — names the object of the attack in its § Context: “By 1551 however, the Sultan of Johor Alauddin Riayat Shah II disregarded the peace treaty and without provocation forged a coalition with the Sultan of Pahang, the Sultan of Perak and the queen of Jepara in Java **to attack Portuguese Malacca**.” That the city was held and not merely sacked is the other end’s own article, “Capture of Malacca (1511)” at revision 1373484620, § Aftermath → The fortress: “Contrary to Sultan Mahmud Shah’s hopes, Albuquerque **did not intend to just sack the city, but to hold it permanently**”, with a fortress whose garrison was 500 men. `precondition-of` and not `caused`: the 1551 article gives the coalition’s own reasons as a disregarded treaty and no provocation, and makes the conquest no part of why the sultans moved in that year — the conquest is what made Malacca a Portuguese city to besiege, not the occasion of the besieging. The two records are siblings under `malay-portuguese-conflicts`, not parent and child, so A14 does not bar the edge. `probable`, on the two articles alone (rule 22).

The same condition, read for the Dutch siege of 1606. “Malay–Portuguese conflicts”, at revision 1370627478, gathers both ends of this edge into one series and says what the Dutch admiral found at Malacca: in § Later conflicts → Siege of Malacca 1606, “In 1606, Dutch East India Company admiral Cornelis Matelief besieged Malacca with the support of the ruler of Johor”, and “The small Portuguese garrison, under the command of André Furtado de Mendonça managed to hold out” — a Portuguese garrison in the city because, in the same article’s § Portuguese Conquest of Malacca 1511, “Albuquerque subsequently **built a fort**, established various institutions in the city, and confirmed religious freedom to its inhabitants.” The same article closes the series by measuring the possession from the conquest: the 1641 siege ended “nearly **130 years** of official Portuguese presence in the region”, which counts back to 1511. The second author is “Capture of Malacca (1511)” at revision 1373484620, the revision that record cites, for the intention the possession rested on: Albuquerque “did not intend to just sack the city, but to hold it permanently”. `precondition-of`: the Dutch came for a Portuguese city, and the conquest is what made it one. It is not a reason the Dutch came in 1606 — that is the Johor alliance and the Company’s war, which the atlas files this siege under as `dutch-portuguese-war` — so `caused` would overstate it. **This edge, the one to the 1551 siege and the one to the 1640–1641 siege share a single argument** and are three records of it, one per siege of the city the 1511 conquest created; they are not three independent findings. `probable`, on the two articles alone (rule 22).

The siege that ended the possession the conquest began, and the one place the articles state the span outright. “Siege of Malacca (1640–1641)”, at revision 1370743206 — the revision that record already cites — opens: “The siege of Malacca (3 August 1640 – 14 January 1641) was initiated by the Dutch East India Company and their local ally, Johor, **against Portuguese Malacca**”, and its § Background says when Malacca became that: “Malacca, established by the Malays in the 1400s, was a significant hub of trade toward the beginning of the 16th century. **It was conquered by the Portuguese Empire in 1511**”. “Malay–Portuguese conflicts” at revision 1370627478 closes the arithmetic from the other side: the siege ended “nearly 130 years of official Portuguese presence in the region”. `precondition-of` and not `caused`: the 1640–1641 article puts the roots of the conflict in the Dutch arrival of the late sixteenth century and the Company’s years of attempts, not in the conquest; what the conquest supplies is the Portuguese Malacca the siege was against. `probable`, on the two articles alone (rule 22).
explanations.capture-of-penon-of-algiers-1529--battle: Charles V sailed on Algiers in 1541 to take back a city the Ottomans had held since 1529, and the 1529 article says so in those words. “Capture of Peñón of Algiers (1529)”, at revision 1370609401, § Aftermath: “Over the following years, Barbarossa used Algiers as a major base for launching raids from the Barbary Coast. The huge Algiers expedition undertaken by Charles V in 1541 to retake Algiers ended in failure.” The second author, “Battle of Algiers (1541)” at revision 1375834500, § Background, dates the possession the expedition set out to undo to the same year: “Algiers had been under the control of the Ottoman emperor Suleiman the Magnificent since its help in 1529 by Hayreddin Barbarossa.” The type is `precondition-of` and not `caused`: what the 1529 capture supplied was the thing to be retaken, and neither article gives it as Charles’s motive — the 1541 article names that separately, as revenge for the siege of Buda, which this atlas does not hold. `probable`, on the articles alone (rule 22).
explanations.capture-of-tunis-1569--conquest-of-tunis: Tunis was the target Don John chose in 1573 because the Spanish fort there had been under siege since the capture of 1569, and the 1573 article gives that as the reason for the choice. “Conquest of Tunis (1573)”, at revision 1370612771, § Background: “A new grand campaign was cancelled with the disbanding of the Holy League and the negotiations between the Ottomans and the Republic of Venice, leading the Spanish Monarchy to ponder about a new conquest in Africa. Knowing the Spanish garrison in the La Goleta fort in Tunis was still besieged since the 1569 capture of the city by Occhiali, this was the chosen target.” The second author, “Capture of Tunis (1569)” at revision 1370609762, carries the recovery from the other end: “The Christian forces were able to recover Tunis in 1573 however the Ottoman forces under Uluç Ali conquered Tunis yet again in 1574.” `precondition-of` rather than `caused`: the same paragraph gives the campaign’s cause as Lepanto’s momentum and the collapse of the Holy League, and the 1569 capture as what made Tunis the place to spend it on. `probable`, on the articles alone (rule 22).
explanations.conquest-of-tunis-1534--conquest-of-tuni: Charles V’s expedition of 1535 was a counter-offensive against Barbarossa’s capture of Tunis the year before, and the 1534 article uses that word. “Conquest of Tunis (1534)”, at revision 1370612766: “Barbarossa thus established a strong naval base in Tunis, which could be used for raids in the region, and on nearby Malta … In 1535 however, upon the plea of Muley Hasan, Emperor Charles V mounted a counter-offensive and retook the city in the conquest of Tunis of 1535.” The second author, “Conquest of Tunis (1535)” at revision 1375228138, § Background, puts the same answer in the verb: “Barbarossa established a strong naval base in Tunis … Charles V was informed that should Barbarossa remain in power in Tunis, both Italy and Spain might be threatened by the Ottoman navy. He therefore assembled a large fleet to drive the Ottomans from the region.” `reacted-to`, running forward in time from the capture to the answer to it. `probable`, on the articles alone (rule 22).
explanations.conquest-of-tunis-1535--capture-of-tunis: What Uluç Ali took in 1569 was the Spanish-installed Hafsid Tunis that the conquest of 1535 had put there. “Conquest of Tunis (1574)”, at revision 1370612776, § Background: “In the next year, however, Holy Roman Emperor Charles V had launched a major expedition and captured it in turn. He established a garrison and a vassal ruler in the person of Lhacène of the Hafsid dynasty. The Bey of Algiers Uluj Ali Pasha captured Tunis in 1569 for the Ottoman Empire.” The second author, “Capture of Tunis (1569)” at revision 1370609762, names both halves of that settlement as what the campaign met: “Uluç Ali encountered the Hafsid sultan at Beja, west of Tunis, Uluç Ali defeated him in battle and conquered Tunis without suffering any great losses. Mulay Ahmad III was forced to take refuge in the Spanish presidio of La Goletta in the bay of Tunis.” The type is the weakest of the five on purpose: **neither article states a motive for 1569**, only the object of it, so this is `precondition-of` — there was a Spanish-backed Hafsid Tunis and a Spanish presidio beside it to be taken because of 1535 — and it is not written as `caused` or `reacted-to`. `probable`, on the articles alone (rule 22).
explanations.conquest-of-tunis-1573--conquest-of-tuni: The Ottoman fleet of 1574 came to take back what Spain had taken the year before. “Conquest of Tunis (1574)”, at revision 1370612776, opens: “The conquest of Tunis in 1574 marked the conquest of Tunis by the Ottoman Empire over the Spanish Empire, which had seized the place a year earlier.” Its § Background names the seizure answered: “in the aftermath of the 1571 Christian victory at the Battle of Lepanto, John of Austria re-conquered Tunis in October 1573.” The second author, “Conquest of Tunis (1573)” at revision 1370612771, § Consequences, reports the answer and the opening it used: “However, Occhiali would retake Tunis the following year due to the disbanding of the Spanish fleet.” The type is `reacted-to`, the retaking of a place lost; the second article’s “due to” names the disbanding of the Spanish fleet, which is an opportunity and not an event this atlas holds, so it is quoted for the fact of the retaking and not as the cause. `probable`, on the articles alone (rule 22).
explanations.fall-of-tenochtitlan--battle-of-colhuaca: The assault was launched because the siege was going nowhere. The Battle of Colhuacatonco article's lead: "The battle was fought as a result of the Spanish soldiers growing dissatisfied with the lack of progress done during the siege thus far, as the Spanish-Tlaxcalan forces had failed to take any important amount of territory since the beginning of June. Captain Hernán Cortés of the Spanish decided to launch a massive assault onto the city to take the market of Tlatelolco." The Fall of Tenochtitlan article is this atlas's record of that siege, which it dates from 26 May to 13 August 1521. `caused`: the article says "as a result of" and names nothing else. It also says what this edge does not: "the battle did not stop the city from falling to the Spanish Empire in August of the same year", so nothing here runs the other way. Probable: Wikipedia alone, at two revisions.
explanations.governorate-general-of-brazil-1549--dutc: What the West India Company took in 1630 was not an empty coast. It was a royal colony with a capital, a government, a church and a working sugar economy — the thing the captaincies had failed to produce and the crown had installed in 1549. A colony is worth conquering when somebody else has already built it, and the Company took the built part: at its height it held almost half of the settled European area of Brazil, with its headquarters at Recife.
explanations.hereditary-captaincies-of-brazil-1534--g: This one is a cause and the sources say so plainly. Four donees never took possession, four more were driven out by the people already living there, and of fifteen grants only Pernambuco and São Vicente prospered. With most of the captaincies failed and French ships working the coast, John III turned the colonisation of Brazil back into a royal enterprise and sent Tomé de Sousa out in 1549 with written instructions and a capital to found. The governorate is what the crown did about the captaincies.
explanations.hereditary-captaincies-of-brazil-1534--t: The captaincies failed as an administration and succeeded as a land settlement: they put the coast into private hands in very large pieces, granted with everything on them, and it was on two of those pieces that the first engenhos were built after 1542. A plantation is a unit of property before it is a unit of production, and the traffic that later supplied it had somewhere to deliver to because of how the land had been cut up. The type is the weak one: the grants did not bring the trade about, they are what it arrived into.
explanations.indigenous-depopulation-of-coastal-brazi: The colonists began with enslaved indigenous labour — the brazilwood was cut by it, São Vicente prospered on it, and the bandeirante expeditions were raids for it — and they moved to enslaved Africans. The sources give both halves: that the shift happened, and that the population being drawn on was collapsing at the same time. The claim is about the shift and not about the whole traffic: what the collapse caused was the turn to an Atlantic supply, and the scale that supply reached was the sugar economy’s doing.
explanations.italian-campaign-of-1524-1525--battle-of: The campaign article makes the battle the thing the campaign ran into: "After the French invaded Lombardy, the campaign would then primarily consist of the French attempt to capture the city of Milan. However, after Francis's defeat at the Siege of Pavia, the French were driven out of Italy and Francis was taken prisoner." The two are siblings here and not one inside the other — both name the Italian War of 1521–1526 in their own P361 and neither names the other — so the edge says what the article says: the campaign is what brought the French army to Pavia. The sentences are not footnoted to any work Wikipedia names, so Wikipedia is the only author and the confidence stays probable.
explanations.italian-war-of-1542-1546--italian-war-of: The Italian War of 1542–1546 article ends on what it left undone: Charles came to terms with Francis at Crépy in 1544, the treaty was made moot within a year by the death of the Duke of Orléans, Henry fought on to the Treaty of Ardres in 1546, and "the deaths of King Francis of France and King Henry VIII of England, in early 1547 left the resolution of the Italian Wars to their successors." The 1551–1559 article opens on one of those successors doing exactly that: the war "began when Henry II of France declared war against Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor, with the intent of recapturing parts of Italy". A war that settles nothing and passes the quarrel to the next reign is a precondition of the war that reign fights, not its cause. Probable, because both articles are read at one revision each and neither names a historian for the reading.
explanations.la-noche-triste--battle-of-otumba--preco: Otumba was fought by the army that had just got out of the city, on the road it got out along. The Battle of Otumba article's § Background: "Cortés then started a retreat to Tlaxcala, during which his force was harassed by Aztec skirmishers, and the Aztec leadership resolved to eliminate them as they withdrew", and its § Battle opens "After being beleaguered on the causeway leading out of the city, the surviving Spanish forces arrived at the plain of Otumba." The Fall of Tenochtitlan article says the same: "Before reaching Tlaxcala, the scanty Spanish forces arrived at the plain of Otumba Valley (Otompan), where they were met by a vast Aztec army intent on their destruction. The Aztecs intended to cut short the Spanish retreat from Tenochtitlan and annihilate them." `precondition-of`: the flight is what put the two armies on that plain, and no article says the flight caused the battle to be fought. Probable: Wikipedia alone, at two revisions.
explanations.massacre-in-the-great-temple-of-tenochti: Both articles make the massacre the reason the city rose, and the rising is what the Spanish fled. The Fall of Tenochtitlan article, § Aztec revolt: "The massacre had the result of resolutely turning all the Aztecs against the Spanish and completely undermining Moctezuma's authority." The massacre's own article closes its lead with the consequence: "When Cortés and his men returned, the Mexica drove the Spaniards out of the city on the so-called the Sad Night (La Noche Triste), losing most of their men in battle or as prisoners who were then sacrificed." The La Noche Triste article states the intervening step — "In retaliation, the Aztecs laid siege to the Spanish compound" — which is the siege the flight broke out of. `caused` rather than `precondition-of`: the articles use causal language for it and name no other reason for the revolt. Probable: Wikipedia alone, at two revisions.
explanations.new-laws--battle-of-inaquito--preconditi: Iñaquito’s article gives the New Laws as what raised both armies: “The said viceroy arrived with the strong intention of enforcing the recently enacted New Laws that abolished the encomienda prohibited the personal labor of the indigenous people. The encomenderos (the masters) protested and organized a rebellion, choosing Gonzalo Pizarro as leader”. The viceroy who fell at Iñaquito was sent to enforce them and the man who killed him was chosen to resist them, which is the same account the atlas already holds for Jaquijahuana two years later. `precondition-of` and not `caused`: the laws set the quarrel, not the battle. `probable`, because the only source the atlas can open here is the article (rule 22).
explanations.new-laws--battle-of-jaquijahuana--precon: The article states the New Laws as what put Gonzalo Pizarro’s army together: “De la Gasca landed in Peru in 1547, winning supporters to his initially inferior forces by promising amnesty to those having committed treason to the crown, and proclaimed he would not enforce the New Laws, whose dispositions demanding better conditions for native laborers had led many powerful encomenderos to join Pizarro’s cause.” The same article has Charles V send Blasco Núñez Vela to Peru “to ensure the accomplishment of the New Laws enacted in 1542”. So the two sides that met at Jaquijahuana are the two sides of the New Laws, and de la Gasca won by suspending them. `precondition-of` and not `caused`: the battle is the end of a revolt the article dates from 1544, four years on, and the laws are its standing cause rather than its occasion. `probable`, because the only source the atlas can open here is the article (rule 22).
explanations.portuguese-landfall-in-brazil-1500--indi: The cause the source names first is disease, and disease arrived with the ships. That is what makes this a `caused` and not a weaker type: the decline from two or three million to three hundred thousand does not begin before contact and is not attributable to anything that was already on the coast. The Tupiniquim who met Cabral in April 1500 are the first named people in the sequence. Nothing about the landfall was designed to produce it, and the atlas has a type for a consequence nobody intended, which is this one.
explanations.portuguese-landfall-in-brazil-1500--the-: Nothing about 22 April 1500 predicts the trade. For thirty years afterwards Portugal sent almost nobody, and what it came for was a dye-wood cut by indigenous labour working for knives and mirrors. The edge is `precondition-of` and not `caused` for exactly that reason: the landfall is the beginning of a Portuguese presence on that coast and of nothing else, and every later step of this chain had to have that presence first.
explanations.siege-of-cusco--battle-of-abancay--preco: Abancay’s own article says why Alvarado’s army was in the field at all: “Alonso de Alvarado, sent by Francisco Pizarro to relieve the siege of Cusco, was camped at Jauja with five hundred men. He guarded the bridge and a ford on the Rio de Abancay, awaiting Almagro’s men.” The force Almagro captured almost intact is the relief column the siege called out, and the article’s next paragraph turns on Almagro “emerging as the victor both in the siege of Cuzco and from initial disputes between the Pizarro brothers”. `precondition-of` and not `caused`: the battle’s own turn is given as Pedro de Lerma’s desertion at the ford, not the siege. `probable`, because the only source the atlas can open here is the article (rule 22).
explanations.siege-of-cusco--battle-of-ollantaytambo-: The Ollantaytambo article gives the raid its reason in so many words: "As a result of these events, neither side was able to break the deadlock at Cusco for several months, so the Spaniard garrison decided to make a direct attack on Manco's headquarters at the town of Ollantaytambo, 70 km northwest of the city." The lead says the same: "To end the stand-off, the besieged mounted a raid against the emperor's headquarters." `caused`: the deadlock at Cusco is what the article says produced the expedition, not merely what preceded it. Probable, and with a second author: the sentence carries Hemming, The Conquest of the Incas, p. 206.
explanations.siege-of-florence-1529-1530--battle-of-m: Both articles name the same quarrel and the siege is what created it. The siege, at revision 1370741144: "They overthrew the Republic of Florence and installed Alessandro de' Medici as the ruler of the city." Montemurlo, at revision 1370450375: "the forces of the newly installed Duke Cosimo I of Florence defeated a hastily organized army of those who wished to overthrow the Medici and restore the Republic of Florence." The party beaten in 1537 is the party the siege put out of power in 1530, and the two records are filed under different wars, so this is an argument and not the filing said twice. Neither sentence is footnoted to any work Wikipedia names, so the confidence stays probable.
explanations.siege-of-naples-1528--battle-of-capo-d-o: The Capo d'Orso article says what put the two fleets in the same water: "A French fleet inflicted a crushing defeat on the fleet of the Kingdom of Naples under Spanish command in the Gulf of Salerno, where Spanish forces trying to break the French blockade of the city met the French fleet." The blockade is the siege this atlas holds, and the sentence makes it the reason the Spanish fleet sailed at all — so the edge runs from the siege to the battle it produced. **It was first written the other way round and the validator refused it**: rule 4's arrow of time, because the siege opens in April 1528 and the battle is the 28th of that month, which is the source saying the battle happened inside the siege rather than before it. The siege is not this battle's parent — the battle's own P361 names the War of the League of Cognac — so this is an argument between two records and not the filing said twice. The sentence is not footnoted to any work Wikipedia names, so the confidence stays probable.
explanations.siege-of-padua--battle-of-polesella--pre: The War of the League of Cambrai article runs the two together in one paragraph: the defenders "managed to hold the city until Maximilian, growing impatient, lifted the siege on 1 October and withdrew to Tyrol with the main part of his army", and then "In mid-November, Pitigliano returned to the offensive, recapturing Vicenza, Este, Feltre, and Belluno... Angelo Trevisan organized a river attack on Ferrara by the Venetian galley fleet, but the resulting Battle of Polesella ended in another defeat for the Republic when the Venetian ships anchored in the Po River were sunk by Ferrarese artillery." The Polesella article says the same fleet "was moored on the river Po, waiting for the right moment to attack Ferrara". `precondition-of`: holding Padua is what freed the Venetian counter-offensive the river attack was part of; the article does not say the siege caused the attack to be made. Probable: Wikipedia alone, at two revisions.
explanations.siege-of-padua--battle-of-the-citadel-of: The Vicenza article states the sequence as a consequence: "the Venetians resisted and in October, after the defeat in the Siege of Padua, the French Army’s Marshal Jacques de la Palice left Veneto, retreating to Milan … The Venetians were now able to take back a large part of Veneto during November and, on November 26, the inhabitants of Vicenza opened the doors of the city." The French withdrawal after Padua is what let the Venetians reach Vicenza at all; the citadel action is what was left once they were inside. `enabled` is the word "now able to" says. Probable: Wikipedia alone, and the sentence carries no citation of its own.
explanations.siege-of-padua--siege-of-asola-1516--pre: The Siege of Padua article closes on exactly this interval: "The defeat was a major loss of face for Maximilian, and the Holy Roman Empire would not attempt another invasion of Italy until 1516." The Siege of Asola article is that attempt: "In 1516, Emperor Maximilian I decided to descend on Italy, eager to regain Lombardy and with it Milan", and it ended on 19 March "with the retreat of Maximilian I, who retreated towards the Tyrol" — as Padua had. `precondition-of`: the failure at Padua is the state the 1516 descent begins from, and the article dates the next attempt by it rather than claiming the one brought the other about. Probable: Wikipedia alone, at two revisions.
explanations.siege-of-tripoli-1551--attack-on-zuwarah: The Knights sacked Zuwarah because they had lost Tripoli the year before, and both articles say so. “Attack on Zuwarah”, at revision 1370429622, § Background: “After the Ottoman Conquest of Tripoli in 1551, the loss created anger in Malta. After the Maltese garrison leader, Gaspard de Vallier, arrived in Malta, he was heavily rebuked, stripped of the habit of the order, and imprisoned. … After spring had passed, the rumor had died, and the Knights began to resume offensive operations against the Barbary Coast. The Knights of Malta were in shortage of sailors and laborers for the work in fortifications. The Knights targeted the city of Zuwarah.” The second author, “Siege of Tripoli (1551)” at revision 1370746050, § Aftermath → Attempts to retake Tripoli, puts the two in the same sentence: “The Hospitallers began making plans to recapture Tripoli shortly after they lost the city, and they raided its hinterland in 1552. That year, a Hospitaller force landed at Zuwarah and began to sack the town, but the knights were repelled and were forced to retreat by an Ottoman counterattack led by Murad Agha.” `reacted-to`, running forward in time from the loss to the raid that answered it. `probable`, on the articles alone, which rule 22 keeps below `consensus`.
explanations.spanish-conquest-of-guatemala--battle-of: The same paragraph carries the second half of how Alvarado got to Acajutla, and it is the allies and not only the road: "After subduing the highland Mayan city-states of present-day Guatemala through battle and co-optation, the Spanish sought to extend their dominion to the lower Atlantic region of the Nahuat-speaking people whom his translators called 'Pipils,' then organized as the powerful state of Cuzcatlán. The Kaqchikel Mayans, who had long been rivals of Cuzcatlán for control over their wealthy cacao-producing region, joined forces with Alvarado's men and supported his campaign. Accompanied by thousands of Kaqchikel warriors, Alvarado then marched on Cuzcatlán." Enabled: the Guatemalan campaign is what gave the march its base and the Kaqchikel who made it an army, which is more than the order in which the two happened.
explanations.spanish-conquest-of-guatemala--spanish-c: Guatemala is where the campaign against El Salvador came from, and the article says so twice. Of the first expedition: "The first campaign against the native inhabitants was undertaken in 1524 by Pedro de Alvarado. Alvarado launched his expedition against the Pipil province of Cuzcatlan, also known as Nequepio, from the Guatemalan Highlands, but by July 1524 he had retreated back to Guatemala." Of what held the province afterwards: an expedition from Nicaragua "marched on San Salvador, before being repulsed by a relief force sent from Guatemala", and the province ended "a colonial backwater with a small Spanish population, within the jurisdiction of the Captaincy General of Guatemala". Precondition-of and not caused: the conquest of Guatemala is the base the Salvadoran campaigns were mounted and resupplied from, not the reason they were mounted.
explanations.spanish-conquest-of-iberian-navarre--sie: The Fuenterrabía article gives the occupation as the reason there was anything to retake: "The siege of Fuenterrabía took place in 1523-24 by a Spanish army, after a Franco-Navarrese army had taken it in 1521 in a new incursion to reconquer the Kingdom of Navarre, which had been occupied since 1512 by troops from the unified Crown of Castile and Crown of Aragon." The conquest of 1512 is the record this atlas already holds, and the siege is not filed under it — its own P361 names the Italian War of 1521–1526 — so this is an argument between two records and not a restatement of the filing. The sentence is not footnoted to any work Wikipedia names, so the confidence stays probable.
explanations.spanish-conquest-of-the-aztec-empire--ba: The article opens its antecedents with the commission and where it came from: "Hernán Cortés, after conquering the city of Tenochtitlan, capital of the Aztec empire, delegated the conquest of the territories southward to his lieutenant Pedro de Alvarado, who set out with 120 horsemen, 300 foot soldiers, and several hundred Cholula and Tlaxcala auxiliaries." Enabled and not caused: the fall of Tenochtitlan is what put a Spanish commander, his men and his Cholula and Tlaxcala auxiliaries on the road south at all, and the article claims nothing more for it than that — the fight at Acajutla is Alvarado's and the Pipils'.

The expedition is why the punitive force came. The Battle of Cempoala article's § Background states it plainly: "While Cortés was enriching himself by leading an expedition in eastern Mexico, he tried to convince the King of Spain, in a series of letters, to take away Cuban governor Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar’s control over the campaign. When Velázquez heard about this, he was furious. He decided to send Pánfilo de Narváez to regain control of the expedition." The Battle of Otumba article says the same thing from the other side: "Velázquez, angered at Cortés' disobedience, sent an armed force at the command of Pánfilo Narváez against Cortés to bring him to justice and claim the lands and riches he had conquered." `precondition-of` and not `caused`: the conquest is the state of affairs the battle could not have happened without, and neither article says the conquest brought that battle about — what did was Velázquez's decision. Probable: Wikipedia alone, at two revisions.
explanations.spanish-conquest-of-the-aztec-empire--ne: The article names the two conquests as what the legislation of 1542 followed: **"following the Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire and the Spanish conquest of Peru, more stringent laws to control conquerors' and settlers' exercise of power, especially their maltreatment of the indigenous populations, were promulgated, known as the New Laws (1542)"**. The New Laws' own article gives the same reading, crediting "denunciations and calls for reform from individuals, such as the Dominican friar Bartolomé de las Casas".
explanations.spanish-conquest-of-the-aztec-empire--sp: The article makes the Mexican campaign the position Honduras was invaded from: “The conquest of Central America that followed was effectively an extension of the campaign that overthrew the Aztec Empire; Cortés himself took an active part in the conquest of Honduras in 1524-1525.” The same section says where the expeditions came from — “These expeditions were launched southwards from Mexico and Guatemala, and northwards from Panama and Nicaragua” — and that “In 1523, Hernán Cortés organised two expeditions towards Central America from Mexico”. `precondition-of` and not `caused`: the article gives the conquest of Honduras its own occasion, Gil González Dávila’s arrival in March 1524 and the jurisdictional quarrel between rival Spanish colonies, and what the Aztec campaign supplied was the men, the base and the licence. `probable`, because the only source the atlas can open here is the article (rule 22).
explanations.spanish-conquest-of-the-inca-empire--new: The other half of the same sentence: the more stringent laws of 1542 were promulgated **"following the Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire and the Spanish conquest of Peru"** — the conquest of Peru being the campaign this atlas holds as the Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire, which the record's own article calls "also known as the Conquest of Peru". The article adds what happened when the laws met the conquest they answered: in Peru the viceroy's attempt to implement them "so soon after the conquest sparked a revolt by conquerors against the viceroy".
explanations.spanish-conquest-of-the-kingdom-of-q-uma: The Petén article measures its own subject against the highland conquest: "Nojpetén fell to a Spanish assault on 13 March 1697, more than 150 years after the conquest of the rest of the Yucatán Peninsula and more than 160 years after the conquest of the Guatemalan Highlands," citing Jones 1998 at p. xix, and its lead says that "in the first half of the 16th century, Spain established neighbouring colonies in Yucatán to the north and Guatemala to the south. Spanish missionaries laid the groundwork for the extension of colonial administration in the extreme south of Petén from 1596 onwards." The colony of Guatemala that the fall of Q'umarkaj opened is what the seventeenth-century entries set out from — the article's own map of them is captioned "Spanish entry routes to Petén during the 17th century". `precondition-of` and not `caused`: the same article gives the delay's reasons as "a combination of its geographical remoteness and inhospitality and the fierce reputation of its Maya inhabitants", so the highland conquest is what made the approach possible and not what set it off. **The two are not the same size**: this edge's `from` is the fall of the K'iche' capital in 1524, which is the decisive event of the highland conquest the Petén article names and not the whole of it, and that is the whole of why this is `probable`.
explanations.the-atlantic-slave-trade-to-brazil--aber: By the 1840s Brazil was the last great market in the Atlantic and the law against the traffic there — the Brazilian law of 1831 — had never been enforced. That is what the Act was for and what it names. The causal claim is the plain one: the persistence of this trade, at this scale, is why a foreign parliament legislated to have its ships taken. The Act’s first result was to enlarge what it attacked, since buyers stocked up against the coming suppression and the heaviest arrivals of the whole traffic fall in 1847 to 1849.
explanations.the-atlantic-slave-trade-to-brazil--lei-: The long edge in this chain, three hundred and forty-eight years end to end, and the weakest type on purpose. The traffic did not bring about its own abolition; a movement, a princess regent and a parliament did that. What it did was determine what there was to abolish — the largest enslaved population in the Americas, built by five and a half million landings — and therefore why Brazil was the last country in the hemisphere to act and why, when it acted, it did so without compensating anybody. An edge of this length is here to be argued with, which is what its explanation is for.
explanations.the-atlantic-slave-trade-to-brazil--proc: A different claim from the one above it, and worth keeping apart from it. That edge says abolition was the trigger; this one says what the Empire was standing on. The political base of the monarchy was a slaveholding agrarian elite, and that class is the traffic’s product: it existed in that form, on that scale, because five and a half million people had been landed to work for it. The Republic of 1889 is the political form that followed the removal of that base, which is a statement about 1540 as much as about 1888.
explanations.the-atlantic-slave-trade-to-brazil--the-: The commodity changed and the institution did not. The early coffee industry was dependent on slaves: a million and a half enslaved people were imported in the first half of the nineteenth century to work the plantations, and when the foreign traffic was outlawed in 1850 the planters turned to European immigrants because the supply had stopped, not because the demand had. `enabled` and not `caused`: what called coffee into being was demand in Europe and North America, and the traffic is what made it possible to answer at that speed and that price.

Gold was found in Minas Gerais in the 1690s by men who had walked there, and what turned a find into a cycle was that half a million enslaved Africans could be brought to the region to work it — against some four hundred thousand Portuguese. The traffic was already running and already organised when the strikes happened, which is why the type is `enabled` rather than `caused`: it did not put the gold in the ground or send anyone to look for it, but a mining economy on that scale was not available to a colony that had to recruit its miners.
explanations.the-brazilian-sugar-cycle--dutch-brazil-: The Dutch Republic did not conquer the north-east of Brazil because it was there. It conquered the part of it that made sugar, held it for twenty-four years with the West India Company’s headquarters at Recife, and lost the value of it in the fighting: Wikipedia’s account has the occupation itself precipitating a decline in Brazilian sugar, with the disruption of production standing beside the rise of planting in the Caribbean. The sugar is both the motive and, in the end, what the war spent.
explanations.the-brazilian-sugar-cycle--the-atlantic-: The colonists began with enslaved indigenous labour and moved to enslaved Africans, and the sources are direct about why: sugar was the colony’s principal export until the early eighteenth century and slave labour was what drove its growth. This is the strongest type in the chain and it is meant strongly. The demand did not merely permit the traffic; the size, the direction and the timing of the traffic are the sugar economy’s, and when the export cycle changed — to mines after 1690, to coffee after 1830 — the traffic changed with it.
